Service ownership and consolidation

Keep one signed GateFox background item and consolidate only proven-owned legacy jobs.

Return to the managed service overview.

The name macOS shows

For CLI-only installations, macOS names a LaunchAgent item after the first ProgramArguments entry, and shows that name in System Settings, Login Items, under "Allow in the Background", and in the "Background Items Added" notification. Since 0.4.7 the installer writes ~/.local/bin/harness-gateway as the managed launcher, plus ~/.local/bin/gateway as a second launcher with the same contents (both set GATEWAY_COMMAND to the harness-gateway path), so every plist written from either command names harness-gateway. The service, desktop login, native relay (its --gateway argument) and consolidated plans all use it. The login environment agent (0.4.7, and a standalone registration today) runs <state>/harness-gateway-login-env, a private script, instead of launchctl, so it is not listed as "launchctl" either. With the unified service it does not exist since 0.4.8. The launchd labels stay com.edihasaj.subscription-gateway*.

Older plists keep working, and a rollback to 0.4.5 needs no plist change: the checks that read a plist's arguments (service plans, login consolidation, consolidation collection, uninstall) accept both .../bin/gateway and .../bin/harness-gateway. A running standalone native relay whose plist names bin/gateway in its --gateway argument counts as the same registration as one written now within the same release, so gateway native install there no longer asks you to uninstall it first; across releases the relay path differs too and the existing refusal stands. An existing harness-gateway link to gateway is replaced by the launcher file; any other file with that name is left alone and the installer refuses to continue. Plists name harness-gateway only while that file carries the installer's marker line; otherwise they keep gateway.

Migration is one-time and happens when a plist is next written by 0.4.7:

  • A standalone service: gateway service install, which upgrades the running service when it is idle like any other install.
  • gateway service consolidate --apply and --next-login write a newly unified service with the new name. They do nothing to a Mac that is already unified.
  • gateway desktop register rewrites the standalone desktop login agent and, without a unified service, the login environment agent.
  • An already-unified service (a service-plan.json exists, as on every production Mac): gateway service install renames the launcher in the service plist file, and in the desktop login plist if one exists. It changes only the first program argument, writes atomically, keeps the label, and does only that and what it always did (start the service if it is not loaded or has no process). It never boots out, restarts or replaces a running service, and it rewrites a file only when it carries the gateway's marker and names a managed gateway launcher whose sibling harness-gateway is managed too. The result says programRewritten: true|false (and desktopRewritten), and appliesAt: "next login": launchd reads the file at its next load, so the running service keeps its current definition until you log in again (or restart through launchctl bootout and bootstrap), and shows the new name from then. appliesAt is "now" when that same call had to load a stopped service. Run it once per Mac after installing 0.4.7.

At the first load of a renamed plist macOS posts one "Background Items Added" notification for harness-gateway, and the old "gateway" entry disappears from the list once the old definition is no longer loaded, which is the next login for a unified service. The signed native app can attribute the existing gateway job to its fox identity without registering another job or restarting the service. See macOS background identity. This association does not change service ownership or replace consolidation.

Preview and apply consolidation

Preview the existing installation:

gateway service consolidate

The preview changes no files or processes. It lists the jobs that would be replaced and the components that the single service would own. It excludes CI, unrelated LaunchAgents, app-owned executors, and unknown job names. Jobs must carry the gateway's management marker. The earlier MacBook Pro 2 tunnel is also recognized by its original label and loopback endpoint.

Apply during a maintenance window:

gateway service consolidate --apply
gateway service status
gateway doctor

Finish chats on this machine and every client using it first. Application refuses an open ChatGPT app or busy inference. An idle inference snapshot cannot prove that a remote chat between inference steps has finished. Explicit application stops the old transports, so it briefly disconnects clients. The command does not quit ChatGPT or change native account settings.

The migration saves the original plists in private service-backups storage, starts the supervisor, and checks its components. The inference HTTP listener must respond; the native relay must report a fresh connected status. When a failed startup proves that the new supervisor is unloaded, rollback restores the previous jobs. Each restore step runs on its own, so one failing step cannot leave the other jobs stopped, and launchctl bootout of a job launchd no longer has (3: No such process) counts as already stopped. When rollback cannot prove the replacement unloaded (replacement_still_loaded), the new service stays running instead: rollback leaves the supervisor plist and the service plan in place, keeps that plist equal to what the loaded supervisor is running (it does not overwrite it with the old job that shared its label), and does not restart the old jobs, so two sets of writers never run together. Superseded plists move to Trash only after the replacement starts, so in that case the old non-service plists are still in ~/Library/LaunchAgents, next to the running supervisor, and their text is saved in the backup. Move them aside (for example to Trash) and reload, or rerun gateway service consolidate --apply, or uninstall the service, so a later login never loads a duplicate. The original error is reported, followed by the names of any rollback steps that failed, and a startup timeout names which readiness condition never held (status_not_current, components_not_running, inference_unhealthy or native_relay_not_connected). The installed native binary replaces earlier test paths while retaining the original relay home and connected-machine registration.

With the unified service the gateway has exactly one background item, harness-gateway. ChatGPT can start at login before this service has set CODEX_CLI_PATH, so the daemon (gateway daemon) runs /bin/launchctl setenv CODEX_CLI_PATH <registered wrapper> as its very first step, before consolidation, any wait or any child. It does so only when the registration receipt names this gateway's own executable wrapper, the release runtime exists, and the login session holds no value or one of the gateway's own wrappers; a foreign override is never replaced. The 0.4.7 login environment agent, com.edihasaj.subscription-gateway.desktop-env (harness-gateway-login-env in Login Items), is no longer written next to a unified service, and the service's desktop component removes a managed one it finds, so a 0.4.7 Mac loses that extra item at its first 0.4.8 service start. A standalone gateway desktop register (no unified service, no pending login plan) keeps the agent. Consolidation does not collect it into the plan, and gateway desktop unregister and gateway uninstall remove any that is left. See the registration section.

Child lifecycle and recovery

The supervisor retries failed children with a delay that grows from one second to thirty seconds. A child failure does not replace the other children. An inference or tunnel child that exits within a minute of its start five times in a row is reported once as component_failing and keeps being retried, so a fault that passes heals by itself. Desktop login setup exits after success. Logs and the component status file are private. The status file is advisory: a write that fails (a full disk, a read-only folder) never stops the service, is reported at most once a minute as status_write_failed, and the next heartbeat five seconds later writes it again. A lease prevents two supervisors from owning the same state directory. Launchd restarts the supervisor and retains ownership of its child process group. The supervisor also runs the watchdog heartbeat (health) for the configuration its plan names, and stops it, with any smoke run in progress, when the service stops. Every self-heal event is listed in diagnostics.

Restart and uninstall

gateway service restart requires the same maintenance window. When the running plan has no inference component (a Mac moving from client-only to standalone), the window skips the inference health check because nothing listens yet. The inference child must accept its own idle guard before the supervisor stops its other components. When a Claude component is configured, the supervisor always declines that idle restart, so the command refuses up front and says why.

gateway service restart --force is the explicit operator restart. It still requires the maintenance window (ChatGPT quit, inference idle), then has launchd stop and start the service (launchctl kickstart -k): the supervisor's SIGTERM path drains inference for GATEWAY_SHUTDOWN_DRAIN_MS and stops every component, including Claude components, which can interrupt Claude work. It waits up to a minute for the new process and reports restart: "forced"; a plain restart reports restart: "idle". Use it to adopt an installed release when Claude components hold the automatic move, then confirm with gateway rollout --verify.

gateway service restart --interrupt is the same launchd restart without the maintenance window or the client-only inference guard: it runs while ChatGPT is open, remote chats are connected or inference is busy, ends every running turn, and reports restart: "interrupted". It is the way out of a service that cannot find an idle moment while chats are refused (gateway rollout says blocked: release_skew); a release that forwards never needs it.

gateway service uninstall explicitly stops all owned components and moves the plan and LaunchAgent to Trash. Provider credentials remain. A job launchd has already dropped (launchctl bootout reporting 3: No such process) can be absent while its process still drains. Legacy standalone installation requires both job removal and process exit before replacement or rollback; see service installation recovery.

Shutdown drain

On SIGTERM or SIGINT, inference stops listening at once and lets running requests finish for GATEWAY_SHUTDOWN_DRAIN_MS (default 4000, clamped to 0 to 5000). The LaunchAgent sets only PATH, and service plans allow only PATH and SSH_AUTH_SOCK, so the variable applies to a foreground gateway serve. A managed service uses the default unless launchd's user environment sets it with launchctl setenv GATEWAY_SHUTDOWN_DRAIN_MS <ms>, which lasts until logout and takes effect the next time the service starts. Requests not yet admitted (queued, still uploading, or loading configuration) fail at once with a retryable upstream_unavailable "Gateway is restarting; retry shortly", and no provider call is made, so nothing is paid for twice. Requests still running at the deadline end the same way and are not reported to GlitchTip. Codex retries them against the restarted server. The inference process itself leaves the drain plus 1.5 seconds after the stop began, after it has recorded the requests still running (a failed ledger row with the usage received so far); the supervisor gives it the drain plus 2.5 seconds before SIGKILL, and closes the shared execution host after inference exits, which takes up to 2.5 seconds more. A stop with a busy stream therefore takes at most the drain plus 5 seconds: 9 seconds by default and 10 seconds at the maximum, within the 10-second timeout that service install, uninstall and consolidation give launchctl bootout. Reverse SSH tunnels and the native relay still stop at the same moment as inference, so streams from other Macs do not get the drain. The drain deadline in cli.ts and the supervisor take effect only after a service or inference restart; an in-place upgrade keeps the running process's previous deadline.

Tunnel and native registration

After consolidation, gateway tunnel install and gateway native uninstall refuse changes that would create competing jobs. gateway native install installs no job either: it only registers the relay the service already runs, for a relay slot that waits as not_registered. It uses the plan's own relay binary, relay home, native home and app CLI, refuses while ChatGPT is open, runs the relay's --check and --enable against the existing, enabled Codex Desktop registration (it never enrolls a new machine), and then writes <state>/native-registration.json. The service starts the relay at its next five-minute check while ChatGPT stays closed. Their status commands inspect the unified service. Desktop registration can refresh the launch environment without creating another login job. Transport changes other than tunnel removal currently require stopping the unified service and registering the required components again before reconsolidation.

Remove an owned tunnel

Retire one tunnel the unified service owns:

gateway tunnel uninstall --tunnel-id spark

This edits the service plan rather than registering another LaunchAgent. It refuses a tunnel name that is not in the plan, and it refuses a component of that name that is not a tunnel. Repeating a removal that already landed reports alreadyRemoved instead of failing again. A repeat is recognised only from the removal record the command writes after the plan edit succeeds (service-backups/tunnel-removals.json, private), by an exact comparison of the recorded tunnel id, and only while the plan file is the one that removal left (the record stores its content hash, inode, modification time and change time, so even a copy with identical content and modification time is another file). Removing another tunnel with this command keeps earlier records valid; restoring a saved plan, editing it by hand, replacing it, or gateway service uninstall followed by a new consolidation ends them, so such a plan reports No tunnel <id> again. A backup file by itself, whatever its name, proves nothing: a failed edit, or a plan someone changed by hand, never makes an unknown name look removed, and spark-2026 never makes spark look removed. If only the record write fails, the removal still succeeds and the result says a repeat will not be recognised. A record that cannot be read counts as no record, so an unknown or repeated name is still refused as No tunnel <id>.

Before it writes anything, it runs the same maintenance check as gateway service restart on a unified plan and consolidation: the ChatGPT desktop must be quit, and when the plan runs inference, /health must answer with status ok and no active inference (a busy, unhealthy or unreachable gateway is refused). The refusals say Quit ChatGPT normally after local and remote chats finish or Gateway inference is busy or unhealthy, each followed by the tunnel was not removed; they do not use the consolidation wording. A plan with no inference component, and a remote-client configuration, have nothing listening locally, so no probe is made and it never depends on the tunnel being removed. A remote-client configuration is never probed even when its plan still lists an inference component (a Mac that moved from standalone to client).

It checks the tunnel's local listeners, which are its -L and -D forwards (also written as -o LocalForward or DynamicForward, attached to the flag, clustered like -NTL, or with a bracketed IPv6 bind). It reads the ssh arguments with the same option table the service uses for ssh (so -P tag and -PLab are a tag, not a forward) and stops at --. It also asks /usr/bin/ssh -G with the same arguments what ssh resolves (it does not connect), and merges that with the arguments: forwards that -F or the host alias add through ssh_config count as the tunnel's own, and so does GatewayPorts. Because ssh -G evaluates the ssh configuration, a Match exec line in it runs, as it does whenever that tunnel starts. A reverse -R forward only listens on the other machine, so it is not checked. It refuses when:

  • a configured provider's baseUrl connects to one of those ports, naming the provider; point that provider at another endpoint or remove it from the gateway configuration, then repeat the removal. A forward bound to loopback (the default) is reached through every spelling of this machine: localhost (with or without a trailing dot, and *.localhost), the whole 127.0.0.0/8 range, 0.0.0.0, ::, ::1, and IPv4-mapped forms such as [::ffff:127.0.0.1]. A forward bound to every interface (*, 0.0.0.0, an empty bind such as :port, any other non-loopback bind address, or GatewayPorts yes or -g without a bind address) is also reached through this machine's hostname and interface addresses. That name counts in either spelling: the full hostname() (Mac-Studio.local) or its bare first label (Mac-Studio), and an interface address counts in its IPv4-mapped spelling ([::ffff:192.0.2.7]) as well as in the dotted one. A provider host that is a name is also resolved (the system resolver, so DNS and /etc/hosts, every address it returns), but only when its port is the tunnel's: any loopback address reaches a loopback forward, and a loopback or own-interface address reaches a wildcard one. So qwen.internal mapped to 127.0.0.1 is refused, and one that resolves to a remote address is not. A lookup that fails or takes more than 3 seconds fails with Cannot determine whether provider <id>'s host <name> reaches tunnel <id>'s local port <port>; the tunnel was not removed, because the answer is unknown. A slow lookup is refused after 3 seconds, but the resolver call is not cancelled, so the command can still take until that system lookup ends to exit. A provider that plainly matches is reported before any name is looked up;
  • on a remote client, one of those ports is the configured port, because that tunnel is how the client reaches its gateway; stop the client with gateway service uninstall instead. Another tunnel on the same machine still retires normally;
  • the tunnel's local port cannot be determined, because the checks above cannot run: a forward's port cannot be identified (a socket path, a malformed spec, port 0, which asks ssh for a free port), a trailing -L, -D or -R has no value, or ssh -G cannot resolve the arguments (for example an unreadable -F file). It fails with Cannot determine tunnel <id>'s local port; edit the service plan manually;
  • the component's command is not /usr/bin/ssh (for example a hand-edited plan that runs autossh or a Homebrew ssh), because its options would be read with OpenSSH's table and guessed. It fails with the same Cannot determine tunnel <id>'s local port error;
  • neither the arguments nor ssh's resolved configuration declare any forward (no -L, -D, -R, LocalForward, DynamicForward or RemoteForward). It fails with Cannot determine tunnel <id>'s local port, like the cases above;
  • the tunnel is the plan's only component; uninstall the gateway service instead;
  • a next-login consolidation is pending (service-login-pending.json): the command fails with Tunnel startup is staged under the unified service at next login before it looks the tunnel up in the plan or changes the plan, whatever well-formed tunnel id was given, so the staged plan can still be activated. The check runs again under the plan lock and the login lock, so a consolidation staged while the command waited for either of them is refused too.

The plan it replaces is saved first to a private service-backups/tunnel-removed-<id>-<timestamp>.json file. The re-read, the check that the plan did not change since it was read, the backup, the plan write and the record all happen under the same plan-file lock service shared-executors, service shared-native and their disable commands hold, so a concurrent change is never overwritten: the removal refuses with Gateway service plan changed, or waits up to 5 seconds for the lock and then fails with Gateway service plan is busy; the tunnel was not removed. The removal takes the plan lock first and the login registration lock second, the order service shared-executors, service shared-native and their disable commands use, so it never holds the login lock while it waits for the plan lock. The commands that move the plan itself are not plan-lock writers: service uninstall trashes the plan and service consolidate --next-login stages one, each under the login lock alone, so a plan that was moved or staged while this removal waited is caught by that second lock and refused instead of written back. A lock that cannot be created at all (for example an unwritable state directory) fails with Cannot lock the gateway service plan (<code>); the tunnel was not removed, or Cannot lock the gateway service registration (<code>) once the plan lock is held; a login lock still held after 5 seconds fails as Gateway service registration is busy; the tunnel was not removed. The (<code>) suffix appears only when the system reports an error code; a lock file that is not a private regular file owned by you gives the same message with no code. Either way nothing was backed up or written. A plan write that fails after the backup leaves the backup in place and records nothing, so a plan someone later edits by hand is still refused as No tunnel <id>.

Nothing restarts: the result says appliesAt: next service restart, and a repeat says the same. The tunnel stops when the unified service next starts from the shorter plan. That is any restart, not only one you run: gateway service restart, a self-upgrade restart after an update, a launchd restart after a crash, or the next login. Until then gateway tunnel status --tunnel-id <id> shows component: null because the tunnel is gone from the plan, but its ssh process keeps running. Restore the saved file over service-plan.json and restart to bring the tunnel back.

Consolidate at the next login

Consolidation is opt-in. Installing an updated CLI prepares the command but does not migrate a running service or interrupt an open chat.

To keep current work running and consolidate the next login instead:

gateway service consolidate --next-login

This saves the original jobs and a private pending plan, prepares one gateway LaunchAgent, and moves its superseded owned startup files to Trash. It does not unload or stop their currently running services. Native and SSH connections keep their processes until logout. The one remaining entry starts desktop setup, inference, native relay, and required tunnels as applicable to that machine. Unrelated apps and CI jobs remain registered.

The new daemon promotes the pending plan only when launchd identifies it as the primary gateway job and every retired gateway job is unloaded. This prevents a manual start from creating competing relays or inference listeners. Activation uses the same configuration, native home, relay home, and connected-machine registration. Pending consolidation blocks separate registration changes that could recreate duplicate startup jobs. Repeating staging is safe after its file checks pass. Startup-file count and macOS's cached Login Items display are separate checks; historical records can remain visible after registration ends.

Staging records which process staged. If that process is gone before the staging finished (a crash, a reboot, or a rollback of its own that failed), the gateway LaunchAgent can still start at the next login with an unfinished preparing record. The daemon starts only from the staged LaunchAgent, so the staging got as far as its last file write and missed only its ready mark. The daemon therefore finishes it first: it runs the same checks as for a ready record (the staged LaunchAgent is unchanged, no retired job came back or is still loaded, no other gateway job appeared, and launchd runs this daemon as the primary job), promotes the plan, logs login_consolidation_completed, and runs it. A check that cannot run at all (launchctl or the disk failing) changes nothing, and launchd's next start tries again. So do the two checks that only mean "not yet": a retired job that is still loaded, and a start that is not launchd's primary job (a manual start). They fail this start and keep the record, so a fully staged consolidation is never rolled back for timing.

Only a check that refuses rolls the staging back. The daemon puts back each original login job whose saved copy still has the digest recorded at staging, writes the private mark <state>/service-login-recovered.json (its boot and the restored job labels), and only then moves the record into the backup as login-recovered.*.json, so a daemon that stops between the two rolls back again at its next start and one that stops later finds the mark. It then loads every restored job except the primary one with launchctl bootstrap, so tunnels, the relay and desktop setup run in this session; a job that is already loaded is left alone, and one that fails to load is counted. Every relaunch in the same boot loads, again, each restored job that is still not loaded, so a daemon that stopped before its loads finishes them. login_consolidation_restored reports how many jobs were put back, started and failed. The primary job, normally inference, cannot be loaded while the daemon holds its label, so inference stays down until the next login or the recovery below. The daemon has no plan to run and stays idle. Every relaunch in the same boot (a crash, launchctl kickstart -k, a stop) finds the mark and stays idle too, instead of failing every ten seconds, and an idle-restart SIGUSR2 does not end it. A saved copy that changed stops the rollback with the record kept, as it does for repeated staging. A staging process that is still alive keeps the old refusal. Records written before 0.4.4 name no process; the login lock the staging holds throughout is the proof that it is gone.

Rollback recovery

To recover after a rollback without logging out:

  1. Check that it happened: the service log has the line an interrupted next-login consolidation was rolled back, and <state>/service-login-recovered.json exists.

  2. Replace the idle daemon with the restored primary job:

    launchctl bootout gui/$(id -u)/com.edihasaj.subscription-gateway
launchctl bootstrap gui/$(id -u) ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.edihasaj.subscription-gateway.plist

    When the staging had no original primary job, there is no plist to load; the bootout alone stops the idle daemon.

  3. Run gateway service status and gateway health to confirm inference answers.

  4. Stage again with gateway service consolidate --next-login when you want the unified service. A promoted staging removes the mark.

Repair disabled jobs and SSH forwards

Explicit tunnel installation and desktop registration enable their managed LaunchAgent before loading it. This repairs a disabled registration without restarting an already loaded job. New tunnel jobs limit the initial SSH connection to one ten-second attempt; launchd or the unified supervisor retries after failure. Existing active tunnel arguments stay unchanged until a maintenance update. Adopted Claude reverse forwards record an owned child/start identity and its verified remote sshd listener, start stamp and TCP peer. A reconnect can clear only that exact former listener after the original client has exited. Missing proof, changed settings, foreign owners and unreadable state preserve the port. Controller adoption records already-running forwards without interrupting them. This recovery uses one bounded SSH probe at connection startup, no extra daemon, and currently records direct IPv4 SSH connections on port 22. Unsupported routes remain conservative. Generic same-user port cleanup stays disabled for Claude. The unified supervisor also adds these defaults when it starts a newly owned SSH child from an older plan. Explicit command-line timeout and attempt values, forwarding endpoints, and SSH profile paths remain unchanged. It does not rewrite the stored plan or replace a running tunnel to add defaults. Network loss can interrupt forwarding, but a loaded KeepAlive job keeps retrying. An unloaded job needs registration again; its plist alone does not start a process in the current login session.
